Recent research shows strong results applying Reinforcement Learning (RL) to generate locomotion patterns for new directions in areas like a new environment or a different morphology. Our experimental results demonstrate that this approach can successfully teach a quadrupedal robot to navigate difficult paths or perform a new behavior, such as a diagonal gallop, at a high speed.

Observing our planet serves as the prerequisite for resolving many global challenges, including those related to climate, food, and health. The widespread adoption of high-resolution remote sensing technologies has enabled us to monitor and analyze this primate's surface, thereby advancing our understanding of it. Although current remote sensing data offers vast educational potential for machine learning models, contemporary approaches continue to struggle. Consequently, many critical and urgent inquiries regarding Earth remain unanswered, prompting a need for more sophisticated training datasets. EarthNets emerges as a solution by providing a collection of networks, each consisting of over one million images and extending more than ten years in history. These observation-specific data structures facilitate large-scale AI research. We make our data publicly accessible at https://www.earthnets.org/.

We perform a real-space renormalization group analysis of two-dimensional active nematics, examining the dynamics near the hydrodynamic nematic-smectic critical point as well as the behavior of pure hydrodynamics as a separate fixed point. Our approach involves perturbing a hydrodynamically coupled idealized lattice model—whose bare coupling exhibits a line of bifurcations—and subsequently identifying the coupling-repairing procedure that transforms this line into an isolated bifurcation point. This modified model is then analyzed to study the coupling's flow under the renormalization group. Renormalization group flow equations are derived, revealing a complex network of fixed points and nematic smectic bifurcation lines. We report the existence of compelling evidence suggesting the presence of additional fixed points that correspond to a phase with hybrid character, blending nematic order with a stripe phase exhibiting quasi-long-range order.

Open-source Software-Defined Networking (ODN) facilitates network modeling and validation before real-time deployment in production environments. Within these production networks, link irregularities such as Link Flapping represent a critical challenge that can degrade user experience and overall system performance. Although existing work focuses on connection anomalies, there is a gap in addressing regional irregularities. Unlike the discrete nature of link anomalies, the spatial extent of link irregularities makes the concept of region instability more effective at prediction and containment. However, defining specific boundaries for these areas remains difficult. The proposed framework ReAD overcomes this limitation by relying on a dynamic partitioning method. Experimental results indicate that the ReAD approach outperforms the state-of-the-art, showing superior precision and recall in identifying unstable regions.

This study performs an in-depth analysis of the pion vector form factor, which has not previously been thoroughly addressed. Using world data on \(\pi^+ \pi^-\) scattering and the world dataset for \(e^+e^- \to \pi^+ \pi^-\), the authors determine the pion vector form factor, \(F_\pi^1(s)\), in the region \(s > 0.75\) GeV\(^2\). Consequently, the contribution of s-channel processes to the anomalous magnetic moment of the muon, \(g-2\), involving high invariant mass is computed. Results indicate that employing the input dataset directly yields a value for \((g-2)^{sc,\pi}_2\) close to previous estimates based on lower \(s\) ranges. Furthermore, the analysis demonstrates that applying a dispersion relation allows for significant reduction of this high-\(s\) contribution.

Although models based on attention represent the state-of-the-art for coding tasks, they rely exclusively on representing individual lines or functions. We introduce a novel approach designed to generate meaningful global representations for entire code projects. By leveraging graph-based architectures, we integrate information across an entire project's structure. Testing with the extensive SWE-Bench dataset demonstrates that a single linear model significantly outperforms current coding assistants, achieving a 4.1% improvement in task resolution. Additionally, we present a multi-stage framework that yields even more robust performance. To examine representability, we run clustering experiments which show that our method effectively categorizes issues according to their root causes. Source code is available at https://github.com/oxlabs/GlobalRepForCode.

We investigate the relationship between stellar mass and dark matter halo mass for galaxies with low to intermediate accretion rates, which are expected to possess the highest halo mass morphologies, and compare these results with a similar analysis of higher-accretion rates and the existing literature. Using the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS-III/MAPS) database, we identify 138,090 galaxies with measured halo masses between $10^{11.5}$ and $10^{12.5}\,M_{\odot}$. The observed $M_{\rm h}(M_{\star})$ trend for these samples aligns with, and is slightly steeper than, that of the broader population. We also present an independent evidence for this specific $M_{\rm h}(M_{\star})$ trend through a comparison of the stellar density profile slopes of $M_{\rm h}(M_{\star})$ galaxies against the overall galaxy sample. The required stellar density profile slopes for $M_{\rm h}(M_{\star})$ galaxies were determined from the mass limits of their respective substructures, which are known to be present in lower-mass halos. The $M_{\rm h}(M_{\star})$ trend is also expected to be independent of halo assembly time, which is an important factor in understanding galaxy formation.

The accompanying discussion summarizes the latest results and outlines new concepts for interpreting aerosol findings derived from stellar observation.

By comparing these enhanced resolution images and corresponding radial profiles to a ground-breaking 000-cm map captured by the CWV Very Wide-band Array, it becomes evident that a pure MHD wind model originating from a disk truncated at 000 AU fails to replicate key features. Conversely, a pure photoevaporation model, using an outer boundary set at 000 AU, provides a robust fit to these key characteristics. Models using intermediate disk outer edges produce structures that do not align as closely. Although model parameters were previously set without optimization through chi-square analysis, the discovery that an intermediate disk outer edge generates a structure more similar to a photoevaporation scenario than to the actual observations further suggests photoevaporation is the dominant disk outflow mechanism.

We introduce an new algorithm that performs both voicing detection and pitch tracking on speech signals, simplifying previous methods by requiring no external information such as voice activity detection or threshold settings, which greatly reduces complexity compared with standard approaches using only energy-based detection. At its core, the proposed method employs a forward-backward Kalman filter to effectively distinguish between voiced and unvoiced segments. By modeling a sinusoidal component alongside noise to represent voicing states, this system accurately tracks fundamental frequency and removes noise during voiced speech, while simultaneously tracking non-pitch noise patterns to correctly label unvoiced segments. Comprehensive tests against various existing techniques confirm that this solution achieves high accuracy and efficiency.

We investigate the effects of radiative corrections on the mass of the lightest CP-even Higgs boson in a next-to-minimal supersymmetric standard model extended with a right-handed singlet exhibiting a Majorana mass (NMSM+RSM). In this framework, the Majorana mass influences the particle's tree-level mass significantly, whereas the resulting two-loop finite mass shifts are subordinate. Our input parameters originate from a global fit across multiple models; specifically, this fit incorporates the RSM sector's specific parameters, including the Majorana mass scale, leveraging LHC constraints under the 125 GeV Higgs discovery context. Additionally, this radiative analysis underpins our previous determination of the Majorana mass scale itself, a variable essential for assessing lepton number violation signatures in future lepton-hadron and colliding machines.

Emerging neural architecture search techniques primarily rely on evolutionary algorithms or reinforcement learning to devise novel network structures. Although these methods yield promising results, they suffer from excessive computing costs and produce designs that may not always align with specific regulatory requirements. Recently, formal synthesis has appeared as a way to generate program instances that adhere to user-defined properties; we adapt and extend the existing program-guided synthesis framework specifically for neural architecture generation. By leveraging this approach, we produce networks that strictly satisfy a defined set of characteristics while reducing training durations. The proposed strategy requires minimal human effort and generates novel, high-performing architectures that were unpredictable prior to design.

Multicasting in millimeter-wave systems is essential for cost-effectively delivering efficient data services to various user categories. Nevertheless, differing requirements and locations pose significant challenges to optimizing resource allocation. Our work introduces a hybrid encoding strategy for multicasting that balances reliability and spectral efficiency, addressing diverse demands from different groups by leveraging pre-shaping and hybrid array encoding techniques. After reducing the resulting non-convex optimization problem to a convex framework, we derive an closed-form algorithm. Additionally, we investigate the performance boundaries of hybrid encoding to highlight its advantages over both orthogonal encoding and naive transmit encoding.

Federated learning (FL) has gained attention as a robust privacy-preserving method for distributed machine learning collaboration, but recent analysis reveals that standard FL can inadvertently leak privacy beyond expected limits. While federatic extraction (FedExp) was previously proposed to address communication privacy vulnerabilities during parameter sharing, communication-efficiency remains an overlooked challenge in this domain. This work introduces a communication-efficient variant of FedExp capable of achieving correct federal extraction with significantly reduced inter-client communication. Evaluation across multiple numerical examples demonstrates that the new approach communication-efficiency dramatically lowers data exchange during collaboration—commensurately less than even the original FedExp.

Network-Driven Computing (NDN) represents a significant evolution in internet architecture, shifting content consumption from centralized servers to on-demand requests via interest packets. Within NDN-based computing environments, achieving optimal workload regulation is essential. To address this, we introduce a control framework capable of independently managing multiple concurrent tasks. Capping total active requests, the system adapts its limits in response to current demand to maintain efficiency, utilizing a specific approach to regulate the peak number of concurrent requests. By modeling the system using two Markov chains and applying concepts from regular variation and heavy-tailed distributions, we derive conditions for stability and provide an explicit formula for the ideal policy. Furthermore, we establish a theoretical framework demonstrating that our proposed policy performance converges to that of full flush strategies under certain scenarios. Numerical simulations further corroborate these theoretical findings.

This paper investigates the stability of an Euler-Bernoulli beam with external localized sources, modeled as a star-shaped network. Our findings demonstrate that under specific boundary conditions, internal control achieves exponential stability. Conversely, in all remaining cases, we prove that asymptotic stability is secured through a robust mixing approach. The analysis further derives optimal times-achieving levels for this infinite-time, zero-dispersion solution stability. These conclusions are supported by a technical outcome of general nature concerning the stability of well-posed evolutionary systems described by linear partial differential equation groups on undirected graphs.

We examine the quark-meson framework, which incorporates explicit explicit chiral-symmetry breaking, to analyze inhomogeneous matter solutions featuring "cubic" and "polar" modulations. Our results indicate that inhomogeneous phases appear in regions of the temperature-baryon density diagram adjacent to the homogeneous phases characterized by either a color-flavor locked (CFL) or nuclear matter structure. As the scale of modulation remains diminutive, we develop an asymptotic expansion for quark distributions and utilize it to derive corresponding conditions for the stability of these inhomogeneous phases.

We investigate new classes of large-gap topological insulators using the $M{Tl}_4{Te}_3$ formula ($M = \text{Hg, Cd}$), and we report novel findings on their structural and surface characteristics. First-priniciples calculations confirm that both the Hg- and Cd-containing compounds exhibit the $R\overline{3}m$ rhombohedral phase as their most stable low-energy state. Surface states for $M{Tl}_4{Te}_3$ with $M = \text{Hg, Cd}$ were examined, demonstrating edge bands typical of 2D Dirac cones alongside surface loops. Furthermore, we identified that $M{Tl}_4{Te}_3$ with $M = \text{Hg, Cd}$ exhibits strong spin-orbit coupling. Finally, we explored their net magnetization effects on magnetocrystalline properties along with their implications for magnetism.

The common strategy for handling multi-objective optimization is aggregating multiple objective functions into a single weighted sum, which necessitates multiple interactive sessions to determine appropriate weights. This approach becomes challenging in practical settings because learning effective weights for unknown, potentially conflicting functions is difficult. To address this, we introduce a differential equation-based approach for estimating effective weights, guided by the principle that effective value distributions should follow the known knowledge of constraints or functions. We further demonstrate that utilizing this effective benefit function to construct the utility landscape enables more efficient search for the best compromise multi-objective outcomes. Empirical results show that the proposed technique can generate satisfactory common objectives in both artificial and practical cases, even without explicit interaction to determine weight ratios.

Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) effectively model sequences by capturing long-term dependencies, making them attractive for developing future attack methods against recurrent reinforcement agents. This study introduces novel transformations aimed at perturbing future states to bias the decisions of the acting agent. The proposed attack strategies are applicable to various agents, including those guided by the temporal difference learning algorithm. Our methods require no prior knowledge of the environment's transition rules, only the agent's previous choices and observed outcomes. The internal decision-recurrence structure is altered without needing its specific model. The success rate of these new attacks is significantly superior to existing non-temporal approaches.

We investigate the electronic properties of a 2D honeycomb-like network lattice featuring second-order non-symmorphic symmetry, which supports a wide array of topological phases governed by its non-symmometric wave vectors. This study demonstrates the existence of numerous topological phases defined by distinct numbers of Dirac points and associated Chern carriers, which can be efficiently explored. We propose an efficient mechanism to adjust both the count and positions of these Dirac points, thereby enabling potential applications involving singular Fermi surfaces in this class of honeycomb networks.

This paper addresses the online reinforcement learning challenge for a risk-averse decision-maker facing time-varying stochastic reinforcement learning tasks with changing probability models. To ensure robustness against uncertainty, we adopt an entropic risk measure. Given prohibitive computational costs in optimizing the exact objective directly, we instead present a nearly optimal dynamic regret guarantee. Our approach relies on a two-step methodology: first, we develop an online dynamic model selection algorithm capable of identifying the best fitting probabilistic structure with guaranteed performance differences; second, we propose a separation-based design for control and identification. Additionally, we introduce a Umbrella Strategy to stationarity, a near-optimal example-specific bound, and discuss implications for fully adaptive strategies.

Software bug reports serve as a primary conduit for communicating defects within private corporate environments, though their scarcity hinders empirical research given the individual nature of most bug data. Furthermore, many projects maintain these entries in isolation, making them hard to assemble into a comprehensive dataset. This paper introduces the SubeBug dataset, assembled from public Jira repositories to overcome the limitations found with private data. It documents the adoption rates of various natural language structures across different projects, with findings indicating that while project-specific variations exist, the overall trends align closely. This consistency ensures that research on one project can yield models applicable to others, and it substantiates the necessity of applying transfer learning in natural language processing tasks related to bug systems.

Distributed machine learning (DML) has emerged as a vital methodology for addressing the challenges of big data. Within this domain, aggregation functions serve a dual purpose of uniting model updates from various workers and ensuring privacy by masking individual contributions. While the standard approach relies on Linear (averaging) aggregation, this method often inadvertently leaks data privacy and unnecessarily constrains design possibilities. This study introduces a new class of non-linear aggregation functions, partitioned into subfamilies based on their mathematical properties, and proposes an efficient DML framework that integrates these innovative functions. To enable effective training, the paper derives closed-form formulas for the gradients of these non-linear aggregation functions and, crucially, establishes an equivalence relationship between them and specific workers' local model updates. Finally, the performance of this proposed framework was assessed against existing algorithms, and the validity of the findings was verified through extensive numerical simulations comparing different linear and non-linear aggregation functions, demonstrating its high validity.

This study introduces an on-chip microfabricated design featuring a sequence of atom trapping gratings designed to guide the path of a single neutral atom. Each interatomic spacing is precisely calibrated to facilitate the capture, control, and detection of individual atoms via two distinct optical pathways, allowing researchers to direct an atom toward specific trapping locations. An electronic switch governs access to these routes, enabling the creation of customizable routing structures that are currently too intricate for natural, non-manipulated setups. Experimental results demonstrate that an $${\ce{Rb}}$$, **atom can be successfully trapped, manipulated, and detected** using this architecture. This novel approach paves the way for building complex quantum circuits and addressing advanced quantum information challenges involving neutral atoms.

This study introduces an algorithm that deduces the molecular masses of a polymers' monomers from the recorded mass-to-charge ($m/z$) ratios of the polymer series. While the input data may contain measurement errors or correspond to an unknown polymer type, our method addresses these challenges. First, we apply linear regression to identify the integer set of possible degrees for each monomer. Subsequently, we execute an integer programming operation to eliminate outliers—an method that yields more accurate results than filtering via standard deviation. Finally, we provide examples utilizing hypothetical polymers and actual experimental data to verify that our algorithm produces outcomes with high precision.

Inelastic neutron scattering (INS) experiments provide access to the dynamic structure factor, $S(\mathbf{Q},\omega)$, which encodes essential information about a material's time- and length-scale resolved excitations. However, extracting this data often involves significant challenges due to the complex experimental setup. As a widely used technique, time-of-flight neutron spectroscopy allows neutrons to scatter off moving target atoms by matching their translational kinetic energy to an object's motion. Isolating this internal motion from other influences is difficult because the incoming neutrons' energy depends on their velocity and flight time.

To address these difficulties, a range of methods has been developed to fit proposed models to $S(\mathbf{Q},\omega)$, successfully identifying specific material behaviors. Yet, these traditional approaches struggle when multiple physical effects coexist and remain non-specific, failing to capture broader physical contexts.

This study leverages machine learning to analyze INS data more comprehensively. The proposed framework is both physical and quantitatively calibrated: it can automatically detect multiple simultaneous effects and quantifies them by estimating their contribution to the signal intensity. Applied to inelastic neutron spectroscopy data, the model offers an interpretable, calibrated neural network capable analyzing effective contributions arising from multiple physical phenomena.

PDFs offer a nonperturbative description of hadrons as a collection of point-like quarks and gluons characterized by a specific momentum scale. Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a prominent framework for training centralized models across distributed datasets, but it faces significant challenges with data non-i.i.d. distributions, which can degrade model accuracy and stability. While Federated Semi-Supervised Learning (FSSL) utilizes limited labeled data alongside abundant unlabeled private datasets to address these issues, most current FL and FSSL algorithms rely on aggregation weight equalization, failing to account for varying degrees of diversity among client data. This study frames FL as a problem of regularized ambiguity reduction and proposes a novel Ambuity-minimizing FL (AmbFL) strategy that adapively balances regularized performance for each client during the learning process, targeting global model optimization. To further accommodate computational constraints in non-centralized environments, we develop a communication-efficient variant called AmbFL-Reduced, which decreases the number of communication rounds. Extensive experiments on popular ML benchmarks demonstrate that both AmbFL and AmbFL-Reduced significantly outperform state-of-the-art approaches, showcasing robust results that hold true for real-world datasets as well.

Numerical simulations of black hole-neutron star mergers represent a significant advancement in numerical relativity and serve as a critical indicator for distinguishing non-detections in gravitational-wave observations. These simulations, which account for effects from general relativity, magnetohydrodynamics, and neutrino radiative transfer, typically model mergers that persist for several seconds or more. We have conducted such simulations across a broad spectrum of initial magnetic field intensities, distributions, and neutron star equations of state. Our results, examined in terms of final remnant fate, ejecta properties, and electromagnetic emission mechanisms, are compiled and discussed. We also developed automated procedures to determine whether an accretion disk forms and whether a compact remnant survives, demonstrating that these novel algorithms are both robust and efficient.

This study addresses the convergence of linear interval arithmetic to the Q-learning algorithm to solve Markov Decision Processes. By defining a novel approach that utilizes linear systems for both value function and policy evaluations, we demonstrate convergence to the optimal Q-function when systems are solved precisely. This research investigates the binding of dielectric nanoparticles within a monolayer of graphene supported by a silicon dioxide substrate. The analysis shows that the characteristic impedance of graphene is dominated by plasmon density, which in turn drives the absorption of incident terahertz radiation. When a nanoparticle approaches graphene, it induces local electric field variations that modify plasmon density, consequently altering graphene's effective conductivity. These changes create an interactive electric field between the particle and the substrate, facilitating electromagnetic-based coupling. The study demonstrates that the interaction energy binding the nanoparticle to graphene is primarily derived from electromagnetic effects. Ultimately, the total interaction energy is calculated to be roughly three orders of magnitude lower than that produced by non-radiative near-field effects, establishing that terahertz electromagnetic interaction serves as a fundamental mechanism for capturing nanoparticles in graphene systems.

Prolonged treatment times within emergency departments are associated with numerous adverse outcomes, including patient deaths. To address this, research has introduced performance metrics that distinguish between time spent on patient care and administrative tasks for greater precision. Administrative activities, however, often reflect general departmental efficiency rather than pure medical performance. Recent efforts aim to normalize these times against specific cases to further refine the analysis. This study proposes a robust statistical approach to averaging reaction curves across entities while accounting for repeated measures and contextual variables. Furthermore, visualization tools accompanying this method enable effective comparison between distinct groups or contexts, thereby assisting administrators in identifying optimizable areas within their operations.

This study explores synchronization strategies for a network of agents performing multiple tasks, designed to maintain desired outputs despite inherent system uncertainties such as disturbances, parameter variations, or unstable dynamics. Each agent utilizes a fully connected graph to exchange information with neighbors, enabling the deployment of distributed control protocols. The primary challenge addressed involves jointly determining optimal control parameters—specifically gain values and timing—for both the synchronization mechanism and the task execution process, ensuring convergence across a system constrained by physical limitations in both processing power and bandwidth. To resolve this, the authors frame the problem within a convex optimization framework and present an alternating minimization algorithm that facilitates the solution of multiple alternatives, including cases where communication and computational constraints are entirely absent.

This difference stems from the higher net baryon density achieved at the lower energy, which favors the conditions necessary for the CME.

The surge in popularity of crowdfunding over the last decade has opened numerous online fundraising avenues for various causes. The authors suggest that while crowd signals do not guarantee victory, they serve as superior predictors of campaign failure compared to outcome metrics, with these findings offering significant value for risk managers and market participants in the broader investment community.

Average-case complexity theory investigates computational hardness within specific distributions of problem instances. A standard approach for defining these distributions is through the recursive self-generating (RSG) framework, which includes many famous distributions and possesses a natural, constrained format. However, this approach faces two primary challenges: limited expressive capacity and fragility. The former hampers rigorous comparisons across diverse distribution families, while the latter means hardness conclusions are typically valid only under minor distribution perturbations, hindering robustness assessments of complexity. To address these issues, we broaden the RSG methodology and demonstrate the rigorous average-case universality and stability of several universal problems—specifically, the shortest vector problem (SVP)—across a diverse range of RSG-induced distribution families. By introducing the novel concept of "tail-contractive" distributions, we identify a substantial category of average-case universal instances for SLP. We also present average-case lower bounds for other key problems, including the closest vector problem (CLV) and integer factorization, within several distribution families. Furthermore, we conclude with a discussion on practical implications arising from these findings.

Radio-loud Active Galactic Nuclei (AGNs) are renowned for emitting a significant portion of the Universe's luminous energy at high redshifts. Despite this, it remains an open question whether their relativistic jets can continue to fuel star formation in massive galaxy clusters throughout the Universe's history, as the effects of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) on energy losses in jet-circumgalactic medium (CMG) interactions are not always accounted for. By employing self-consistent 3D magnetohydrodynamic simulations, we investigate how jets behave when penetrating a galaxy cluster's hot gas across a range of kiloparsec to megaparsec scales, specifically evaluating the impact of the CMB. Our findings indicate that while the CMB is negligible for jet propagation across most redshifts, it becomes a critical factor at high redshifts ($z > 6$). Under these early cosmic conditions, a Lorentz factor $\gamma \approx 5$ yields a CMB-induced loss rate roughly 100 times greater than the rates caused by stellar populations or thermal gas. We investigate the behavior of quasinormal modes near the polymer singularity within a spherically symmetric gravitational field by leveraging the behaviorally complete basis of the non-linear quasinormal mode. To achieve this, we employ a coordinate transformation that redefines the time variable, addressing the behavior of both time and spatial derivatives as one nears the singularity. Using a Taylor expansion for the spatial metric and the behaviorally complete basis, we approximate the nonlinear terms. Consequently, we derive an infinite algebraic system for the quasinormal mode, enabling an investigation into their local behavior at the singularity. Finally, a computationally efficient numerical method is introduced to determine the quasinormal mode frequencies.

Investing in graphene's exceptional qualities requires understanding how its unique properties react to thermal influences. This study explores the impact of screening on quasiparticles in n-type graphene sheets containing excess electrons and calculates the resulting heat capacity for both clean and disordered systems. By applying the self-consistent Born approximation, we address the strong Coulomb interactions inherent to these two-dimensional materials. Our numerical analyses, which depend on temperature, doping levels, and disorder strength, align well with previous studies on quasiparticle lifetimes. Results indicate that increased Coulomb interactions alongside elevated temperatures significantly shorten lifetime. While excess screening reduces life expectancy across all conditions compared to unscreened scenarios, quasiparticles remain largely stable when screening is absent. Consequently, the heat capacity for both pristine and disordered graphene sheets demonstrates only minimal deviation from predictions made by a single-parabola model unless the system is subjected to high temperatures and strong interactions.

Speech generation models are typically optimized for two distinct tasks: speech synthesis, which converts phonemes into natural-sounding utterances, and recitation, which maps full sentences to speech. However, existing models used for these separate tasks often fail to deliver the same high performance. This paper introduces MaskedSpeech, a new context-aware speech generation model that utilizes a masking strategy to improve results. We achieve this by employing a masking method to hide specific sections of the input sentence, thereby training the system to generate more natural phoneme sequences within that limited context than it would with the full sentence. For those context sections that are hidden from the model, a separate reconstruction model is trained to recover the original sentences from those phoneme sequences. Experiments demonstrate that this two-stage approach significantly outperforms current methods and improves results across various datasets.

Estimating the conditional average average treatment effect (CAATE) is essential for conducting policy analysis on unobserved populations of interest. Although recent research has developed projection estimation techniques using data from reference groups, these approaches rely on representing target characteristics through specific features or bases in a high-dimensional data space. We introduce projection predictive estimation (PPE), a fully Bayesian technique that directly projects treatment effects onto a chosen latent space without high-dimensional assumptions. Additionally, we provide a framework for selecting this latent space based on the intrinsic dimensionality of reference and target data structures. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed method competes effectively with state-of-the-art estimation strategies, while also establishing theoretical bounds on its estimation error with minimum assumptions.

While models trained on synthetic data offer a cost-effective and efficient alternative to classifiers relying on real-world datasets, their integrity is vulnerable when adversaries can inject malicious synthetic samples into the training pipeline specifically targeting such systems. This work introduces a new class of synthetic data assaults known as "Generative Model Attacks (GMAs)." We outline the GMA framework and construct robust countermeasures. Our assault leverages bad data labeled with incorrect or suboptimal outputs during training; we exploit this corruption to steer classifier bias toward incorrect classifications for clean test samples. While label poisoning is inevitable and label refinement is energy-intensive and costly, our GMA assumes only a basic ability to poison the label pool. Furthermore, our GMA remains undetectable because the associated attacker generative model only operates during training and never needs to be presented directly to the classifier. Beyond these advantages, our GMA is extremely versatile: we successfully poisoned label generators that range from simple Gaussian generators to GANs and Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), deploying them against three distinct classifier types, including traditional Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE), Quantized Bayesian, and Deep Neural Network classifiers. Through extensive experiments using both real-world and publicly available datasets, we demonstrated the GMA's efficacy and evaluated various solutions—spanning from basic rejection rules to sophisticated detectors, and even the deployment of their GNA counterparts as denoisers—on the classifier front.

Three-body simulations involving protoplanetary discs and hierarchical systems with mass ratios $M_1/M_2=10$ or $M_1/M_2 =1$ demonstrate that flat, non-rotating host systems cause the accretion rate onto the primary star, $\dot{M}_1$, to exceed that of the secondary, $\dot{M}_2$, by up to three orders of magnitude. This disparity is driven by the interaction between the circumprimary disc and its respective Hill sphere. When this prolate sphere is non-rototing and aligned with the line of nodes, it facilitates more efficient accretion for the primary star. Our results suggest that, in such disc-interactive hierarchical systems, the secondary star can gain up to approximately 0.25 solar masses ($\approx$0.25M$_\odot$) of mass, though this figure is modest compared to the required formation of brown dwarfs and stars. However, when comparing these findings to non-disc three-body models, the disc-interactive version is found to more effectively form brown dwarfs and stars around the primary host star.

We explore a three-dimensional $Z_2$ gauge theory defined within a lattice framework. In our study, we observe that when a specific parameter is tuned, the system's phase transition resembles a Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transition. Notably, this transition causes the average absolute values of both the magnetic field ($\langle |B\rangle$) and electric field ($〈|E〉$) densities to vanish at the critical point. Furthermore, the modeled behavior mirrors that of the early universe during its flatness phase. However, it is crucial to clarify that, unlike the actual universe, this phenomenon in the system arises from phase transitions with $Z_2$ gauge symmetry rather than representing a genuine gauge symmetry breaking.

Image segmentation is a fundamental task within image processing that enables objects to be identified and classified through analysis of their characteristics, boundaries, textures, and colors. While numerous methods—including level set, region growing, clustering, edge detection, active contours, and Anisotropic Diffusion—are available, many exhibit limitations regarding computational efficiency or robustness. This study proposes a novel segmentation framework by integrating the curvelet transform with the total variation (TV) derivative, applied across both image details and structural boundaries. Initially, curvelet coefficients of the input image are computed to extract key features; subsequently, these features feed into a model with a dual-energy function designed to separately recover texture and boundary information, ultimately informing the segmentation process. Experimental results demonstrate that this new approach outperforms existing segmentation techniques in accuracy, offering greater reliability and efficiency.

Heavy black holes (BHs) that have settled into a quasi-equilibrium state following recent observations from LIGO/Virgo can function as powerful laboratories for investigating ultralight scalar and vector fields, a hypothesis known as "fairy tale" or better stated here as specific theoretical models where field signatures appear around BHs. The field's presence is typically detected through the spin evolution of the heavy BH when it engages in hard-inhaling accretion processes. In this work, following detailed calculations involving mass and spin constraints derived from hard-inhaling scenarios onto heavy BHs, along previous studies showing how these fields impact the spin dynamics, we derive new constraints specifically on ultralight boson fields such as flat-space scalar fields ($m_\phi=1.5\times 10^{-6} M_{\odot}^{-1}$) or real scalar fields ($m_\phi=1.5\times 10^{-6} M_{\odot}^{-1}$). Specifically, next-generation accretion observations involving heavy BHs are expected to improve current limits derived solely from gravitational waves by several orders magnitude. As such, future projects will likely tighten these boundaries further.

Creating intelligent autonomous neuromorphic systems demands a tight integration of high-level programming interfaces, low-level hardware controllers, and precise simulation tools. We introduce Loihi as a four-generation universal neuromorphic central processing unit designed for research in spiking neural networks. This article presents an initial software emulator built in collaboration with Loihi. Built on Clyde—a general-purpose spiking simulator—this integration yields a high-level neutral API named "brain2," tailored for developing neuron circuits suitable for neuromorphic computing. This paper presents a technical overview of the brain2/Loihi stack and illustrates its utility through real-world examples featuring thousands of neurons and specific spiking patterns.

Utilizing 100-year-old radio observations, we introduce the radio phenomenon of solar noise storms and examine their temporal links to magnetic signatures from microflare events. A decade of 1-GHz data reveals storm durations of approximately a few thousand seconds, with peak power variations spanning orders of magnitude. These events, typically clustered, show temporal correlations with hard X-ray (HXR) profiles from near-microflare scales, including parallel rising and falling phases. A co-occurrence in X-ray emission indicates that a subset of radio storms originate in small magnetic loops. We infer from these findings that plasma heating, compressions, and disintegration of magnetic field lines likely govern explosive communications during solar noise storms, offering a deeper understanding of activated small-scale magnetism and solar dynamics.

Atom-based sensing devices are recognized for their exceptional sensitivity and broad spectrum of applications, yet they remain cumbersome due to the complex vacuum systems and intricate setups needed to capture and manipulate atoms. We have now demonstrated a magnetic optical trap located on a chip that leverages non-reciprocal effects to simplify this process by replacing multiple standing-wave lasers with a single continuous-wave laser source. This innovation not only creates a smaller atomic sensor but also paves the way for further advancements in integrating atom chips.

In this theoretical study, we simulate the evolution of a black hole surrounded by a charged, collisionless plasma confined within a sphere. By analyzing both rotating and non-rotating systems, we determine the black hole's evolving mass and radius as well as the system's angular momentum. Our results calculate four momentum thresholds: two beyond which the angular momentum cannot be fully extracted by the black hole, and two additional limits specific to angles of observation greater than zero where residual angular momentum persists in the outer region. Furthermore, the black hole's angular momentum can exceed the Kerr limit if the outer space contains charged particles holding significant momentum. The study also quantifies the kinetic and potential components of the plasma's energy.

Handwritten document recognition systems are significantly hindered by poor image quality. This study introduces a multi-task adversarial framework, HIDE-GAN, designed to restore low-quality handwritten documents by generating high-fidelity images while preserving the original text content. GAN-driven enhancements have previously been used to create natural-looking variations for single-line handwriting; however, our novel architecture is the first to address multi-line documents effectively. Initially, a content-encoding convolutional network extracts features from the input document. Subsequently, a generator uses this encoded representation to reconstruct the image, employing both a discriminator to ensure visual realism and a uniqueness constraint to diversify outputs. Crucially, we integrate a validity verification step where a recognition model checks if the synthesized images contain meaningful text before finalizing the output. Conducted on 1,200 newly annotated, high-resolution images, our experiments demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms existing enhancement techniques. This superiority holds true even when processing low-resolution multi-image documents not present in the original training sets.

The rise of technology and automation has transformed banking by shifting processes from manual execution to automated systems. One critical area involves verifying customer identities using ID cards, a task currently handled manually with limitations. This study proposes an automated solution leveraging Information and Communication Technology to extract data from ID cards via Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and Natural Language Processing. Implemented in Java, the system successfully extracted information—including names utilizing regex and various data points like numbers—the latter using Java Natural Language Processing. Test results demonstrated a data accuracy of 95%. Ultimately, this methodology stands to significantly improve efficiency within the banking sector's ID management.

The IEEE 802.11p standard facilitates intelligent transportation systems (ITS) by enabling in-vehicle communications, a feature that has attracted the interest of numerous researchers. Within a wireless environment, channel estimation enhances signal-to-noise ratios and data reliability. Although traditional data-driven approaches, particularly Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, have shown great promise in wireless channel estimation, they often struggle to maintain consistent accuracy when processing time-varying channels. Addressing this limitation, this paper introduces a novel, data-driven LSTM framework that incorporates temporal averaging. In this design, the input to the network consists of a set of sub-carriers, each processed through a separate, dedicated LSTM branch, with the final output being an estimate for that specific sub-carrier. The scheme's effectiveness was verified through simulations, demonstrating significant improvements in channels with fluctuating characteristics. When compared to previous methods, this new algorithm reduced the root mean square error by 40% in slowly varying channels and achieved a even more substantial decrease of 55% in rapidly changing scenarios.

We describe a specific colorization project conducted at the Steward Tubing, analyze its outcomes, and discuss the article's broader implications for astronomy.

This study presents a dual metasurface design that successfully mitigates the line ripple interference. By adjusting the radius of a circular ring within the single-layer meta-atom, we achieve dual functionalities: energy trapping and concentration. Dual circular rings allow the line ripple to converge at a specific location. Furthermore, line ripple interference is avoided. For energy trapping, a smaller meta-atom radius creates a strong meta-material effect that guides line ripple along the metasurface. At meta-material resonance, the wave impedance aligns with free space, causing incident electromagnetic waves to enter the structure. Simultaneously, subwavelength spacing between rings isolates the fields, causing energy to be absorbed. To enable field concentration, a larger meta-atom radius shifts the system from a meta-material state to a surface wave regime. Impedance mismatch in this regime funnels energy into the metasurface. Additionally, impinging electromagnetic fields interact with the metasurface as a meta-waveguide, focusing the energy between meta-structures by utilizing curvature. Ultimately, the radius variation within meta-surface meta-atoms provides a cost-effective method to steer line ripple interactions, facilitating diverse applications in optics and photon technology.

We believe that creating scalable, open, and cognitive AI architectures capable of handling large-scale multi-agent systems—specifically those involving humans and robots engaged in collaborative learning—is essential. Such an environment must be able to handle extensive setups involving numerous simultaneous learning interactions. We contend that exploiting nature-inspired approaches based on evolutionary principles is vital to meet this demand.

In support of this view, the document introduces a cognitive AI architecture designed as both flexible and scalable. This framework enables the construction of biological-inspired AI systems on a massive scale for both research and production use. The presentation includes the architecture's initial implementation and a demonstration of its effectiveness through a collaborative learning task executed within a quantum annealing-based platform. We believe this offers a crucial initial step toward developing scalable cognitive AI architectures focused on large-scale multi-agent workspaces featuring human-robot teamwork and on-going learning.

Extracting relations from textual data stands as a pivotal task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), with prior research typically relying on performance enhancements achieved through context window expansion, the inclusion of pre-trained language models, or multi-text ensemble methods. This study proposes a distinct approach that enhances relation extraction capabilities by integrating results from a knowledge graph-based link prediction. Specifically, we employ an attention-based encoder to represent both individual sentences and a complementary Knowledge Graph (KG) through robust textual paths. These enhanced representations feed into a bi-directional recurrent neural network (Bi-LSTM) to establish correlations between sentence structures and KG evidence, which is subsequently optimized using a focal loss function to mitigate class imbalance. The proposed method is evaluated on two standard datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance with exact match scores of 78.9% on clinical mentions and 75.13% on medication mentions within the BioNLP 2014 Clinical Message Shared Task.

Conditional expectation sets form the cornerstone of machine learning task such as classification, regression, and survival analysis, particularly when undergoing distribution shifts. This study introduces a semi-generative framework that utilizes both causal structure and the conditional independence of features given their parents to model these shifts. Utilizing indicator variables to represent the distribution at specific time points, our approach reconstructs the conditional distribution within the Markov partition of the causal graph while simultaneously learning the shift in the top-level covariate. Consequently, this allows for label or label-like information adjustment across covariate shift scenarios. We assess the method on synthetic datasets to verify the correctness of the estimated shift models and on real-world data, including MIMIC-III, further confirming its validity.

Deep learning represents a foundational element of artificial intelligence and remains one of its most outstanding achievements. To ensure community integrity, online social platforms employ safety teams to investigate reported incidents, take corrective actions, and engage with users. Our study centers on a 30-month analysis of a major site's user-reporting system to gain deeper insight into these user-platform engagements. Specifically, we analyzed over 140,000 dispatched tickets and more than 11,000 follow-up comments to unravel the relationships and disagreements between users and moderation staff. While safety teams aim to foster trust, our findings reveal a pattern of conflict characterized by severe misalignment in how each group views the safety process. Between 2014 and 2016, such systems showed an average decline in collaborative activity alongside a rise in issues, even as dispute frequency remained stable. The data also highlights that individual disparities in dispute frequency are extreme, with the most affected users involved in three times as many conflicts as the average. Additionally, the platforms often fail to address the specific issues raising safety concerns, with 38 percent of contentious comments addressing problems that were not part of the user's original complaint. These failures to resolve specific disputes, combined with perceived treatment by safety personnel as malicious or incompetent, have led some users to cease interacting with community management entirely.

Detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) samples is a critical capability in natural language processing (NLL) text classification, with significant implications for security and health. For instance, classifiers for medical text omissions must raise alerts when encountering unfamiliar inputs, as such cases may represent rare conditions. Yet, defining the characteristics of general out-of-distribution samples remains unclear. This paper addresses the classification and management of these instances. First, it categorizes OOD texts based on the prevalent, scarce, and unnatural categories. Using four existing detection benchmarks, it locates the types of OOD text that remain undetected by current methods. Next, it proposes clustering techniques to group similar out-of-distribution instances without relying on label information. Finally, it explores methods for utilizing these clusters to flag potential anomalies. Empirical results indicate that proposed methods offer greater significance in detecting the previously overlooked OOD instances.

The standard pruned DTW algorithm operates by gradually reducing the search area within the distance matrix as it calculates Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) distances. We introduce a new algorithm called **Pruned DTW (prunedDTW)** that performs significantly better than the traditional version by utilizing more granular search area estimation. The key innovation of our algorithm is a more precise method for determining this search area, specifically by **pre-calculating early discarding values** before the main computation to effectively bound the minimum possible distance. Because the approach is simple and highly efficient, our algorithms demonstrate **substantial improvements** over the standard method in the realm of similarity search.

Current research indicates that providing detailed code reviews helps learners acquire effective testing competencies. Nevertheless, delivering individualized feedback proves costly and time-intensive for instructors. This study explores whether generic inquiry-based conceptual feedback can facilitate comparable learning outcomes in software testing, aiming to challenge the prevailing assumption that only thorough feedback is necessary. The study compares inquiry-based conceptual feedback against traditional detailed feedback, measuring their impacts on conceptual understanding and debugging performance among undergraduate students. Results indicate that while both approaches yield equivalent performance on conceptual and debugging tasks, inquiry-based conceptual feedback is significantly more effective at promoting problem-solving skills and offering quicker return on investment regarding feedback costs.

Explainable AI has become a critical field as there is a growing need to understand and trust the decisions made by black-box models. While numerous approaches exist for creating descriptive models of black-box systems, the greatest challenge lies in their inability to offer expressive explanations that account for variations in input data. To address this gap, this study proposes a novel method for generating detailed and dynamic accounts of both deterministic and stochastic Deep Neural Network models. The framework combines a mathematical framework for descriptive model analysis with a method producing explanations based on logical rules. The demonstrated performance of this framework on a image classification model indicates its potential for user trust in black-box systems through transparent rationale.

Over-smoothing represents a recognized limitation of Graph Neural Networks, causing a gradual decline in performance as more layers are added due to excessive aggregation of node information. This paper investigates the root causes of over-blurring, revealing that it stems from two mechanisms: first, an increase in the spectral radius triggers information loss within the high-frequency components of the graph signal; second, these components decay exponentially across layers due to an effect exacerbating the first mechanism. As a result, we establish a theoretical upper limit on how information diminishes through a graph convolutional network. Beyond theory, we offer an effective strategy to detect over-blurring in various graph settings. Empirical results using multiple real-world datasets confirm that our method outperforms prior techniques in both identifying the phenomenon and proposing remedies.

This study details an inquiry into dark matter production during proton-proton interactions at the CERN Large Hadron Collider, operating at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. These observations are interpreted within a framework interpreting simplified dark matter models produced via a $Z$-boson interface. Updated constraints on the coupling constants and mass of the invisible sector have been derived. The reported limits represent the most stringent results obtained by CMS to date within this specific theoretical domain.

Recent research indicates that the anisotropic geometry of three-dimensional (3D) neutrino-supernova models—likely caused by standing accretion-shock oscillations and fast neutrino instability—may generate anisotropic magnetic fields. These magnetic lines are thought to originate from the amplification of the Parker instability, potentially influencing the outcome of the explosion, an effect that is especially pronounced in high-magnetic-magnetization (HSM) scenarios. An in-depth comparison between two-flavor and three-flavor neutrino approaches is necessary to accurately characterize the influence of the fast instability on early-stage dynamics. Additionally, we noted that including NC oscillations results in more efficient cooling in HSM cases than in two-flavor neutrino-SM results during the early phases.

Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) remains a prevalent condition in children and is typically managed through the combined use of medication and behavioral therapy. Despite these treatments, the diagnosis often suffers from subjective inconsistencies, and the condition currently lacks a definitive objective method for assessment or monitoring of treatment responses. This study addresses these gaps following the implementation of the multi-scale attention autoencoder network to analyze rs-fMRI data from 179 ADHD patients and 179 typically developing controls. Our investigation confirmed that the chosen deep learning model outperformed existing methods in distinguishing ADHD states and identifying areas active during therapy. Furthermore, the study mapped the primary brain components involved in classifying both the ADHD condition and treatment efficacy. These initial regions of interest included parts of the cingulate brain structures and several segments within both temporal and parietal areas.

While quantum interference is widely recognized as a fundamental driver of charge transport in mesoscopic systems, its role in thermal transport remains less understood. In this study, we utilize a dual-probe, two-terminal device within a quantum Hall charge pump to experimentally observe heat flow regulation via interference effects. We demonstrate temperature-dependent heat-toggling across a wide thermal range, occurring over cycle periods as short as 10 ms. Additionally, the observed heat oscillations enable heat rectification and diode-like rectification, with efficiency approaching 50%. Such precise control over heat propagation is crucial for the development of next-generation thermal management solutions, particularly within chip systems, and aieses towards advancing in the field of thermoelectric energy conversion.

Encoding data as DNA offers potential for massive data compression and storage through several research studies. Experimental results show that the average time required to update only a single block is less than 1 ms. Finally, the work demonstrates how utilizing binary encoding enables compression rates superior to its text-based alternatives within the same DNA storage context.

This paper introduces a differentiable, Monte Carlo-based algorithm for ray tracing that accurately models shadow effects. Traditional volumetric rendering methods like Monte Carlo ray tracing are accurate but prohibitively slow for gradient-based inverse problem solving that relies on shadow computation. To overcome this, we treat shadow calculation as a global light simulation process and develop an innovative algorithm that integrates shadow testing directly into the standard Monte Carlo ray tracing framework, resulting in a speedup of approximately 3x. We demonstrate the efficacy and superiority of our approach over state-of-the-art techniques by utilizing it as a prior for various inverse problems, including computed tomography, X-ray diffraction tomography, X-ray tomographic histotripping, and deblurring.

This study introduces a new model designed to estimate spatial demand matrices between origins and destinations based on daily transaction records. Day-by-day variations in these matrices are captured through a probabilistic framework that partitions flow distributions into distinct non-zero and zero clusters. By applying Maximum a-Posteriori (MAP) estimation, the model infers the underlying spatial structures and day-specific mean demands. Empirical testing with real-world card data from the Stockholm metro system confirms the model's ability to accurately reconstruct average demand patterns while simultaneously detecting changes caused by events, such as the closure of the metro due to the 2023 European Championships.

We find inertia gradients trigger phase synchronization, which advances along these gradients, whereas equal average inertia distributions result in local clustering. Next we analyze how increased coupling strength can destabilize the local synchronized state, initiating the formation of Synchronized Bursting Waves oscillating. Effective heat exchange between gas and solid components is vital for the success of many industrial chemical reactions occurring within porous beds. While research has extensively covered fluid dynamics in these environments, spatial and instantaneous temperature distributions remain poorly understood. This study introduces a novel methodology that utilizes rapid magnetic resonance imaging (rMRI) to map temperatures in gas-phase flows through solid beds, complementing the technique with a numerical simulation. Both experimental results and simulations reveal that the temperature of the gas varies significantly across the bed and moves dynamically with time. The study confirms that thermal interactions in such beds are governed by the convection coefficients, initial temperature setups, and the material properties of the bed, thereby stressing the necessity of accurately predicting temperature arrangements to optimize industrial heat and mass transfer operations.

This work examines the self-assembly characteristics of open systems featuring multiple components that form various biomolecular aggregates. Specifically, we analyze self-sustaining states where constituent aggregate concentrations remain constant because fluxes are balanced by assembly and disassembly rates. Beyond these, we present general methods to identify stable states and calculate their stability. Application of these principles to a specific model system demonstrates that multiple stable configurations can indeed form. Finally, we assess the functional implications of such multiplicity in terms of signal processing and suggest that multiplexed, multiple stable states could serve as a foundational model for developing efficient multiplexed biomolecular platforms.

The concept of the Integrated Access Backhaul (IAB) was initially conceived to optimize backhaul resources within 5G networks. Although the hyperparameter tuning of optimization algorithms is crucial for their performance, this task remains difficult due to an lack of clear guidelines. Currently, no method exists to evaluate their global impact across an entire family of algorithms, a gap this work addresses by applying global sensitivity analysis techniques. Our findings indicate that GA's parameters have limited global significance, suggesting their specific impact varies greatly and they do not drive consistent performance trends across the algorithm type.

Current reinforcement learning (RL) methods typically assume a single task per learning session and rely on extensive training data before achieving good results. It presents significant challenges due to a vast state-action search space and a sparse, noisy reward system that hinders effective credit assignment. We outline why current RL algorithms fail within this specific context and propose two novel solutions: one based on sparse reward models and a second on dense reward engineering. Our experiments demonstrate that both methods outperform prior alternatives, successfully building a capability to accumulate and utilize experience across a evolving sequence of tasks.

This study examines light transmission through a spherically shaped medium with layered properties, using solutions to the vector Helmholtz equation. We identify specific boundaries within the material that delimit transmission eigenfunctions and investigate their physical characteristics. In dialogue systems, detecting user intent—identifying behind the underlying purpose of utterances—is crucial for grasping (both understanding) the context and crafting suitable replies. Current systems typically lean on methods that either fine-tune on large datasets or utilize encoder-based architectures to extract features for intent classification. Our paper proposes an innovative pre-training scheme that significantly streamlines the process: it pre-trains both separate projectors and their adversarial components on continuous utterances to align contrastively with the ontological categories of intent. By aligning these structures through contrastive learning, we enable a single-stage fine-tuning phase that utilizes the already aligned components. This ability to align without additional optimization steps significantly reduces the overall optimization complexity. Our experimental evaluations on the large-scale Onto10 dataset reveal that we surpass existing cutting-edge baselines.

The Absalom (ABS) $\hbox{H2}$ system stands as a distinct type of integrable component variant related to the Riesz nonlinear wave equation. Visual Relationship Detection (VRD) focuses on identifying semantic interactions between objects in an image. While existing studies primarily address increasing recall by reducing false negatives—often leveraging large datasets—the potential impact of excessive false positives on VRD performance remains largely ignored. This paper provides a comprehensive analysis demonstrating that high levels of erroneous positive detections significantly hinder system performance and real-world applicability. To address this observation, we have developed "Coarse-to-Fine Reasoning for Visual Relation Detection" (CFRWD), a novel approach that enhances relationship verification by exploiting multi-scale contextual information. Specifically, CFRWD is implemented as a post-processing step that refines initial predictions from pre-trained models; it sequentially examines suggestions at both coarse and fine contexts. At a coarse level, it utilizes object-level regions to identify semantic conflicts among proposed relationships, whereas at a fine level, it leverages spatial-semantic image features to filter out precision errors. Experiments conducted on three standard datasets confirm that CFRRD not only boosts overall system performance but also serves as an effective module that raises the accuracy of existing state-of-the-art methods.

We propose the new metric termed Quantum correlation price under a weak measurement, applicable to both classical and quantum contexts. A distinctive feature of this concept is its capability to quantify the degree of disturbance inherent in a specific measurement. Leveraging the defined correlation price, the authors introduce a method to experimentally assess quantum back-action within a quantum system. Consequently, this paper presents a fresh operational framework for measuring quantum state disturbance, thereby extending the relevant concepts into the realm of stochastic thermodynamics.

Social relationships constitute a fundamental element in almost every social network. However, extracting these relationships from raw data, such as text, poses significant challenges because relationship definitions vary widely across different societies and cultures, presenting problems in generalization and portability. To address this, the paper presents an architecture that utilizes a multi-modal approach to extract social relationships by synthesizing evidence from both user tagging and tagging suggestions (which indicate potential tags). The proposed method first employs multi-modal features to represent tags, then leverages a network to process this input, ultimately outputting a Social Relationship Graph.

Communication Receptive Field Networks (CRFNet) represent a recently introduced class of neural networks featuring a communication receptive field (CRF), which enables a node to exchange messages directly with a dynamically selected, uniquely addressable node. To date, however, applying CRFNet to the task of visual recognition has not been explored. In response, this work introduces Dynamic Graph Communication Passing Networks (DGCRFNet), a model derived from CRFNet specifically designed to address visual recognition. We applied DGCRFNet to two core tasks: visual classification and visual localization. Notably, for visual classification, messages are exchanged between nodes representing image patches, whereas for visual localization, communication occurs at atomic units of an organized knowledge graph. Testing on multiple standard benchmarks for visual classification and object localization demonstrated that our approach achieves competitive performance. Particularly for visual classification, the results are comparable to the current state-of-the-art, while requiring only a fraction of the computational complexity.

Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCM) is vital for various fields, including digital signal processing, and modern techniques typically execute these operations using integer arithmetic to combine shifts, adds, and subtractions effectively. Addressing this, this study introduces three novel macro-figures to evaluate the expense of the addition-and-shifting components used in MCMs. Leveraging these new metrics, the authors recast the MCM problem as an search for a multiplication coefficient vector that minimizes a specific linear-weighted combination of arithmetic operations. The proposed solution employs sparse-lexicographical optimization within integer linear programming (ILP). Applying this method yields several novel McCas with notably lower operation counts compared to existing resources.

Secure multi-party computation (SMC) enables distributed parties to jointly execute functions on privately held inputs, and Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) has emerged as a highly promising implementation. Valued Constraint Optimization Problems (VALOPTIMIZATION) involve finding a configuration with superior total values given domain assignments and specific constraints on those domain options. Although the FSOS is proven NP-hard even for trees, the TOTAL VALuated TREEL SUBGRAPH (TVALTS) and MAX TOTAL VALuated BOUNDED DEGENRAT E AVEGAGE (MAX TOTAL VALuated BOUNDED DEGENRAT E AVEGAGE) variants were recently demonstrated as solvable via exact algorithms with runs in exponential time relative to the tree width, prompting a long-standing conjecture that a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) might exist for tree width. This study introduces the concept of SPARSITY OF GENERAL VALuated OPTIMIZATION PROBLEMS and demonstrates that the TVALTS and MAX TOTAL VALuated BOUNDED DEGENRAT E AVEGAGE can both achieve a PTAS through general algorithms designed for these classes.

Pretrained language models offer vast parameter counts that enable significant capabilities across many tasks, though their black-box nature hinders explainability. Instead, it focuses on grouping items based on the internal modeling architecture, identifying which layers facilitate clustering and demonstrating how this knowledge enhances model usage. Consequently, our technique offers a comprehensive, unsupervised map of the linguistic concepts captured by these models.
